oneLiner: 使命答“我们为谁创造什么价值”，愿景绘“我们想成为的未来”，价值观定“我们坚守的原则”。
oneLinerEn: Mission says what value we create for whom; vision paints the future we want; values fix the principles we keep.
detail: 使命、愿景、价值观是组织的最高法院，三者在不同的时间轴上：使命答“我们为什么存在”——为谁、做什么，二十年回头看仍要成立；愿景答“我们要去哪个未来”——十年后一幅可辨认、可描绘的图景，每实现一代就换下一幅；价值观答“追逐途中不越什么线”——在利益与良心的两难里最受检验。三件套的用法不是装点大堂，而是裁断难题：战略取舍、资源分配僵持时回到三问——合不合使命、是否朝愿景近了一步、有没有违反价值观。质量标准很反直觉：一句任何对手都能原样抄去挂墙的使命，是装饰品；好的使命具体到能否决一个赚钱的机会——1982 年芝加哥有人把氰化物注进泰诺胶囊致七人死亡，强生依据信条首句“对医生、护士、患者和父母的责任”，不顾法律义务立即下架回收 3100 万瓶、损失上亿美元，换来此后数十年的信任背书。从未让公司损失过钱的价值观不是价值观，是海报；它们只有在拒绝过金钱之后，才成为文化。
detailEn: Mission, vision and values form an organisation's supreme court, each on its own clock. The mission answers 'why do we exist' — for whom, doing what — and should read true in twenty years. The vision answers 'which future do we want': a concrete, recognisable scene a decade out, replaced each time one is realised. Values answer 'what lines we will not cross in the pursuit', and are tested most where profit clashes with conscience. Their use is not lobby decoration but deciding hard cases: when strategy or allocation deadlocks, return to three questions — does it serve the mission, move toward the vision, honour the values. The quality test is counterintuitive: wording any competitor could copy onto their wall is ornament. A good mission is concrete enough to veto profitable opportunities — when seven people died of cyanide-laced Tylenol in Chicago in 1982, Johnson & Johnson, on its creed's first line ('responsibility is to doctors, nurses, patients, mothers and fathers everywhere'), recalled thirty-one million bottles despite having no legal duty, swallowed over a hundred million dollars, and bought trust that outlived the scandal. Values that have never cost the company money are not values but posters; they become culture only after they have been used to turn down cash.

oneLiner: 把局面摊成四格：优势与劣势(内部)、机会与威胁(外部)。
oneLinerEn: Lay the situation out in four boxes: strengths and weaknesses (inside), opportunities and threats (outside).
detail: SWOT 源自 1960 年代初斯坦福研究所的长期计划研究（常被归于汉弗莱，出处有争议），贡献是把内部的强/弱与外部机会/威胁摆进同一张四格，是战略讨论最便宜、最直观的开场。常见失败是把“填满格子”当完工：格子里是形容词不是证据——“品牌强”强过谁、对哪个客户强；四十条平铺不分主次，等于没有重点；弱点写成“还不够好”的客气话；外部两格三年没换过。正确用法三步：证据标准——优势要能回答“比对手与顾客的其他选项强在哪”，机会要写出“错过它会怎样”；交叉组合（TOWS）——用优势抓机会、补短板乘机会、以优势防威胁、避威胁弃短板，每类组合产出候选动作；最后排序并标注时点——没写“截至何时”的四格分析会风化。四格只负责把问题摆上桌面，桌面下的证据得靠 PESTEL、五力与价值链去收集。
detailEn: SWOT descends from Stanford Research Institute's long-range-planning work around 1960 (credited to Humphrey, though its provenance is contested), and its gift is a four-cell grid sorting internal strengths and weaknesses against external opportunities and threats — the cheapest, most intuitive opening of strategy talk. The standard failure is treating the filled grid as the job done: cells hold adjectives, not evidence ('strong brand' — stronger than whom, for which customers); forty flat items, hence nothing important; weaknesses euphemised as 'room for improvement'; the external boxes not refreshed in three years. Use it in three moves instead. Demand evidence: a strength enters only if it beats competitors and customers' alternatives, and an opportunity must state what happens to us if we miss it. Cross-combine (the TOWS matrix): strength riding opportunity, weakness patched to seize opportunity, strength deployed against threat, weakness-and-threat calling for retreat — each crossing yields candidate moves. Then rank and date-stamp: an undated four-cell analysis fossilises. The grid's job is to put questions on the table; the evidence under the table still has to come from PESTEL, five forces and the value chain.

oneLiner: 判断一个行业赚不赚钱：现有竞争、潜在进入、替代品、供应商议价力、买方议价力。
oneLinerEn: Judge an industry's profit potential by five forces: rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, supplier power, buyer power.
detail: 迈克尔·波特 1979 年的锋利在于把“竞争”从盯对手升级为读结构：一个行业能不能持续赚钱，不取决于它看起来多光鲜，而取决于五股拉扯利润的力量——新进入者的威胁（进入壁垒高不高）、替代品（门外有没有更便宜的解法）、买方议价（客户能不能压价）、供方议价（上游能不能卡你）、现有竞争者的强度（是不是一片价格战）。五力越强，行业回报越被瓜分侵蚀。它的真正用法不是填空而是提问：哪一力在近两年悄悄变强了？壁垒在哪些环节能被主动抬高？战略的意义因此是：选一个结构有利的位置，或用行动改变这些力量本身（如提高转换成本、构筑壁垒）。要防的误区是把五力当静态快照——平台经济、开源与监管常在重切行业边界，十年前的答案今天可能倒转。
detailEn: Michael Porter's 1979 move was to upgrade competition from watching rivals to reading structure: whether an industry keeps earning depends not on how glossy it looks but on five forces tugging at profit — the threat of new entrants (are barriers high), substitutes (is there a cheaper answer waiting outside), buyer power (can customers squeeze price), supplier power (can the upstream squeeze you), and rivalry among incumbents (is it all-out price war). The stronger the five, the more returns get competed away. Its real use is not filling boxes but asking: which force quietly grew in the last two years, and where can barriers be deliberately raised? Strategy then means occupying a structurally favourable position, or changing the forces themselves — say by lifting switching costs or building barriers. The trap is treating the five as a static snapshot: platforms, open source and regulation keep recutting industry boundaries, so the answer of a decade ago may run in reverse today.

oneLiner: 要么更便宜(成本领先)，要么更特别(差异化)，要么更聚焦；卡在中间最难活。
oneLinerEn: Lead on cost, differentiate, or focus — being stuck in the middle is the hardest way to survive.
detail: 迈克尔·波特 1980 年在《竞争战略》里提出：在任何一个行业里，想长期获得高于平均的回报，只有三种连贯的基本定位——在全行业以更低成本取胜、以独特性换取溢价、或收缩进某个足够狭窄的细分战场深耕。三者彼此拉扯，怕的是“夹在中间”：既无成本优势、又无鲜明差异，容易被两头挤压。取舍是战略的灵魂，决定不做什么和决定做什么同样重要，因为定位一旦要通吃所有客户与需求，各项动作就会互相拆台。他后来在《什么是战略》（1996）里进一步强调：战略不是运营效益的堆叠，运营效益是追赶者能抄的，独特且环环相扣的活动耦合才是抄不动的那部分。
detailEn: In Competitive Strategy (1980) Michael Porter argued that within any industry there are only three coherent positions from which to earn above-average returns over the long run: win on lower cost across the whole industry, command a premium through uniqueness, or concentrate on a segment narrow enough to serve better. The three pull against one another, and the trap is being "stuck in the middle"—neither a cost leader nor a differentiator, squeezed from both sides. Trade-offs are the soul of strategy; deciding what not to do matters as much as what to do, because a position that tries to please every buyer and every need makes its own activities undercut each other. In What Is Strategy? (1996) he pressed the point further: strategy is not operational effectiveness piled up—efficiency can be copied by any fast follower—while a distinctive, mutually reinforcing fit of activities is the part that resists copying.

oneLiner: 从政治、经济、社会、技术、环境、法律六个方向，看组织外部的长期大势。
oneLinerEn: Watch six external currents shaping the long game: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal.
detail: PESTEL 把宏观扫成六域：政治（监管风向、地缘、税）、经济（增长、利率、汇率、购买力）、社会（人口结构、生活方式、观念）、技术（新技术的成熟度与成本曲线）、环境（碳、能源、可持续压力）、法律（劳动、消费者、反垄断、合规），有的版本再加伦理一格。它负责给 SWOT 的外部两格供料，但价值不在填满六格，而在逐格追问“这条趋势对我们意味着什么、我们会因此改什么”：出生率本身不是机会，“单身家庭买小包装食品”翻译到决策层才是；六格里最重要的动作，往往是挑出影响力大、不确定性也大的两三根变量，送进情景规划去搭不同未来。三类失败要防：把新闻当趋势（一条标题不是趋势，要看方向、速度与拐点）；只观察不翻译（六格填满、无人因此改做什么）；把快照当结论（每格都该标日期并定期复审）。
detailEn: PESTEL scans the macro in six domains: political (regulation, geopolitics, tax direction), economic (growth, rates, exchange, purchasing power), social (demography, lifestyles, values), technological (maturity and cost curves of new tech), environmental (carbon, energy, sustainability pressure) and legal (labour, consumers, antitrust, compliance); some versions add ethics as a seventh. It feeds the two external boxes of a SWOT, but its worth is not in filling six cells — it lies in pressing each with 'so what does this trend mean for us, and what will we change because of it'. A birth rate is not an opportunity; 'single-person households buying small-package food' is, once translated into a decision. Often the most valuable move is picking two or three variables that combine high impact with high uncertainty and carrying them into scenario planning to build different futures. Three failure modes: mistaking news for trend (one headline is not a trend — look at direction, pace and inflection); observing without translating (six full cells, nobody changing anything because of them); freezing a snapshot into a conclusion (every cell deserves a date and a review cycle).

oneLiner: 用鼓舞人心的目标(O)加两三个可量化、有时限的关键结果(KR)，让全组织朝同一方向聚焦。
oneLinerEn: An inspiring Objective plus two or three measurable, time-bound Key Results keep the whole organisation pointed one way.
detail: OKR（目标与关键结果）由安迪·格鲁夫在英特尔脱胎于德鲁克的目标管理、打磨成一套严格节奏，后经约翰·杜尔引入谷歌并在其推广著作里带向大众。要义是少而聚焦：一个鼓舞人心的定性目标配上两三条可量化、可验证的关键结果，全公司上下对齐又高度透明，鼓励人人看得到彼此在做什么。它敢于设定“野心目标”——拿到约七成即算优秀，故主张与薪酬考核适度脱钩以保护冒险。常见走形有二：把关键结果全写成“照常运营”的任务清单，就退化成了待办事项；或者自上而下硬性分派，就丢掉了它一半价值在于自下而上提报的自主性。它追求的是聚焦与透明，而非又一套考核表格——把 OKR 用作打分工具，恰恰违背了它的初衷。
detailEn: OKRs (Objectives and Key Results) were shaped into a disciplined rhythm by Andy Grove at Intel and brought to Google by John Doerr, who popularized them in Measure What Matters. The essence is few and focused: one inspiring qualitative objective paired with two or three measurable, verifiable key results, aligned top-to-bottom and highly transparent so everyone can see what everyone else is doing. It dares to set "moonshots"—reaching about seventy percent counts as excellent—so it argues for decoupling from pay and performance review to protect risk-taking. Two familiar distortions: write every key result as business-as-usual and it decays into a to-do list; impose it purely top-down and you lose the half of its value that comes from bottom-up proposals.

oneLiner: 不去血腥的红海硬拼，而是用“价值创新”开创让竞争无关的新市场空间。
oneLinerEn: Rather than battle in a bloody red ocean, use value innovation to open a market space that makes competition irrelevant.
detail: 钱·金与勒内·莫博涅 2005 年提出，针眼不在“避开竞争”而在同时拉开成本与价值两条曲线。抓手是“四步动作框架”：对本行业视为理所当然的要素逐项追问——哪些可以剔除、哪些该降到标准以下、哪些该升到标准以上、哪些从未被创造该新建——前两问压成本、后两问抬价值，一气把价优与差异两件难两全的事做成。关键不是技术颠覆，而是重新定义问题与买家：太阳马戏团把“动物表演”这一昂贵核心剔除、把杂耍与故事升为主角，做出了面向成人的新市场。它最容易被误读成“找到冷门就好”：蓝海不是无人区的碰运气，而是价值创新的系统性重建——先问“谁从不买、为什么从不下单”，而不是先盯着对手降价。真正的风险在“蓝海变红海”的速度：模式一旦奏效，模仿者很快涌入，护城河得靠持续重建而非抢先一步。
detailEn: Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne, in 2005, set the pin not on dodging rivals but on pulling the cost curve down and the value curve up at once. The lever is the four-actions framework: for every factor the industry takes for granted ask in turn — which can be eliminated, which reduced well below standard, which raised well above it, and which never offered should be created — the first two cut cost, the last two lift value, achieving low price and differentiation together, the trade-off everyone assumed was fixed. The point is not technological disruption but redefining the problem and the buyer: Cirque du Soleil eliminated the costly core of animal acts, raised acrobatics and narrative to stardom, and made a new market of adults who had never bought a ticket. It is most misread as find a quiet niche and get lucky; a blue ocean is not a gamble on empty space but a systematic rebuild of value innovation — asking who never buys and why they never ordered, not first watching rivals cut prices. The real risk is how fast a blue ocean turns red: once the model works, imitators flood in, so the moat must be a standing rebuild rather than a single head start.

oneLiner: 真正的护城河是能横跨多种产品、难以模仿、为客户带来显著价值的“能力根”。
oneLinerEn: The real moat is a root capability that spans products, is hard to imitate and delivers customer value.
detail: 加里·哈默尔与 C. K. 普拉哈拉德 1990 年在《哈佛商业评论》的《公司的核心竞争力》里用一棵树作比喻：终端产品是枝叶，核心产品是树干，核心竞争力是根——本田小而精的发动机能力同时养出了摩托、汽车、割草机与船舶，德州仪器的精确校准则横跨芯片、显示器与机床。多元化于是变成一堆各自为政的散装生意。判断一条能力够不够核心有三道检验：能延展进多个市场、对手难模仿、客户能真切感知价值。这一概念既指导了自建能力，也为后来“外包什么、自持什么”的取舍提供了标尺。它也提醒：一旦把真正核心的能力外包出去，公司往往连带让渡了围绕它持续创新的机遇，这正是后来许多企业把业务“切回去”的原因。
detailEn: C. K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel, in The Core Competence of the Corporation (Harvard Business Review, 1990), reached for a tree: end products are the leaves, core products the trunk, competencies the roots—Honda's small, precise engines grew motorcycles, cars, mowers and marine motors alike, while Texas Instruments' skill in fine calibration spanned chips, displays and machine tools. They faulted the portfolio analytics then in vogue for asking only whether a unit was attractive, never whether its capabilities fit, so diversification became a heap of unrelated businesses. A competency earns the label "core" by three tests: potential to spawn entry into many markets, rivals' difficulty in imitating it, and a perceptible contribution to the value the customer feels. The idea guided build-versus-buy on one side and, later, the sharper question of what to outsource and what to keep in hand.

oneLiner: 把企业拆成从进料到售后的一串活动，看每一环是创造价值还是消耗成本。
oneLinerEn: Break the firm into a chain of activities from inbound logistics to service, and see which link adds value or burns cost.
detail: 迈克尔·波特 1985 年在《竞争优势》里把企业拆成一条价值链：基本活动涵盖内部后勤、生产作业、外部后勤、市场销售与服务，支持活动则包括基础设施、人力资源管理、技术开发与采购。他认为竞争优势并非凭空而来，而是来自比对手更优地设计与执行这一连串具体活动；更妙的是“链接”——把研发与生产、生产与售后等环节咬合成对手难以复制的系统，在衔接处创造优势。它把“成本”与“差异化”这两大抽象战略落到可逐项审视的活动上，也为后来“哪一段自持、哪一段外包”的决策提供了工具。沿链看，成本与差异化往往藏在环节的衔接处，单看某一部门的高效，可能只是把浪费推给了下一环——这正是局部优化反而伤害全局的老问题。
detailEn: In Competitive Advantage (1985) Michael Porter recast the firm as a value chain: primary activities spanning inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service, supported by infrastructure, human-resource management, technology development and procurement. Competitive advantage, he argued, does not float free but comes from designing and executing this sequence of discrete activities better than rivals; subtler still are the links—meshing R&D to production, production to after-sales into a system rivals cannot copy, creating advantage in the seams. The frame brings "cost" and "differentiation" down from abstraction to activities you can inspect line by line, and hands later managers a tool for the "keep which segment in-house, outsource which" decision.

oneLiner: 用九宫格讲清一家企业如何创造价值、传递价值、获取价值。
oneLinerEn: Nine blocks that state how a firm creates, delivers and captures value.
detail: 奥斯瓦德 2005 年提出这张画布，动机很实际：商业计划书太长，没人读完也没人改。九个格分成两侧：前台五格回答“把什么价值卖给谁、怎么触达、怎么收钱”（客户细分、价值主张、渠道、客户关系、收入来源），后台四格回答“靠什么把它造出来、花多少钱”（关键资源、关键活动、关键伙伴、成本结构）。它真正的本事不是罗列九项，而是让断点可见：为低端客户配了高接触渠道、价值主张依赖一项自己并不掌有的资源、成本结构按固定写而收入按次数收——这些于一页纸上互相打脸。它的局限也要说清：九格是平铺的清单，不表示因果与时间顺序，也无法回答“为什么对手不能复制”——那需要另外一层（盈利公式与五要素说）。实用上它最适合做对比：把自家画布与竞对的并排挂在一面墙上，差异会比任何形容词都直白。
detailEn: Osterwalder proposed the canvas in 2005 from a plain complaint: business plans are too long to read and nobody revises them. Nine blocks fall into two sides. The front answers what value goes to whom, how it is delivered and paid for — segments, value proposition, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams. The back answers what makes it possible and what it costs — key resources, key activities, key partnerships, cost structure. Its real skill is not listing nine items but making breaks visible: high-touch channels assigned to low-end customers, a value proposition resting on a resource you do not own, costs written as fixed while revenue is metered per use — on one page these contradict each other in public. Its limits are equally plain: nine blocks are a flat inventory, encoding neither causality nor sequence, and the canvas cannot answer why a competitor cannot copy you, which needs an extra layer (the profit formula and the five-element reading). Practically it works best as a comparison: pin your canvas next to a rival's on the same wall, and the difference will speak louder than any adjective.

oneLiner: 增长有四条路：市场渗透、市场开发、产品开发、多元化——按新旧产品×新旧市场划分。
oneLinerEn: Four ways to grow — penetrate, develop markets, develop products, or diversify — by pairing new/old products with new/old markets.
detail: 伊戈尔·安索夫 1957 年在《哈佛商业评论》用“产品×市场”两轴把增长选项分四格：卖更多的现有产品给现有客户（市场渗透），把新产品卖给现有客户（产品开发），把现有产品卖进新市场（市场开发），以及新产品进新市场（多元化）——风险沿对角线递增，这是它最耐用的部分。它的价值不在预测，而在逼人把“我们要增长”说成可讨论的具体路径：很多公司的“新业务”拆开看只是换个城市的渗透，而真正的多元化常被当作顺手项目。两个常被忽略的提醒：第一，四格不互斥也不穷尽，纵向一体、平台化、服务化转型都落在格子之外；第二，它不回答能力问题——“市场开发”听起来风平浪静，直到发现渠道、监管与用户习惯全部重来。今天它最好用的场景是开头而非结尾：用它把候选增长拉平、排序风险，再逐格去问资源与证据。
detailEn: Igor Ansoff used a product-by-market grid in a 1957 Harvard Business Review article to sort growth into four cells: more of the same product to the same customers (penetration), new product to the same customers (development of product), the same product to new customers (development of market), and new product to new customers (diversification) — with risk climbing along the diagonal, which is the part that has worn best. Its value is not prediction but discipline: it forces 'we want to grow' into a specific, discussable path, and many a 'new business' unwraps to mere penetration in another city, while real diversification gets launched as a side project. Two warnings commonly skipped. The four cells are neither exclusive nor exhaustive: vertical integration, platform moves, and a shift to servitization all land outside the grid. And the matrix says nothing about capability — market development sounds calm until channel, regulation and habit all have to be rebuilt. Use it at the start rather than the end: lay candidate growth paths out, rank them by risk, then interrogate each cell for resources and evidence.

oneLiner: 获客、激活、留存、推荐、收入——用五步漏斗衡量增长是否健康。
oneLinerEn: Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue — a five-stage funnel for measuring whether growth is healthy.
detail: “海盗指标”是投资人戴夫·麦克卢尔整理并推广的增长框架：它借五个英文字母的首字母，把增长拆成用户生命周期的五环——获取、激活、留存、营收、推荐，并主张每一环都配上可量化的关键指标与北极星阈值。它的锋利处不在记住这五个词，而在逼创业者逐环定数：次日与三十日留存曲线是否走平、病毒传播的系数能否大于一、免费到付费的转化几何，再据此快速定位漏得最狠的那一环。留存常被视作“到底有没有人真正爱用这个产品”的照妖镜——获取可以靠烧钱买来，留存却装不出来；前四环若立不住，最终营收这一环也无从谈起。它因此既是初创公司的增长仪表盘，也是给投资人讲清增长逻辑的通用语言。
detailEn: "Pirate metrics," a framework popularised by the investor Dave McClure, borrows five initials to split growth into the five rings of the user lifecycle — acquisition, activation, retention, revenue and referral — each insisting on its own quantifiable key metric and north-star threshold. Its edge is not memorising the letters but forcing founders to put a number on every ring: whether the day-one and day-thirty retention curve flattens, whether the viral coefficient clears one, how free converts to paid — then to find the leakiest ring fast. Retention acts as the truth serum for whether anyone genuinely loves the product, since acquisition can be bought with cash burn but retention cannot be faked; if the first four rings fail, the final revenue ring has nothing to rest on. It is at once a startup's growth dashboard and the shared language for explaining growth logic to investors.

oneLiner: 把业务摆进“增长×份额”四格：明星、现金牛、问题、瘦狗，据此定投资与取舍。
oneLinerEn: Plot each unit on growth x share — Star, Cash Cow, Question Mark or Dog — and let the box set where to invest or cut.
detail: 布鲁斯·亨德森(1970)为波士顿咨询所创：纵轴市场增长率(要不要输血)、横轴相对市场份额(有没有造血)。明星两头高，应加码；现金牛低增长高份额，挤现金去养别人；问题高增长低份额，是赌未来的选择题；瘦狗两头弱，通常剥离。它给多元化公司一张“资金从哪来到哪去”的简明地图；局限是“份额=优势”与“增长=吸引力”并非万能，故常与 GE 九格(改用行业吸引力/竞争力两轴)互补。
detailEn: Bruce Henderson's 1970 matrix for BCG: vertical is market growth (whether to feed cash), horizontal is relative share (whether it generates cash). Stars are high on both — invest; Cash Cows are mature with high share — milk them to fund others; Question Marks grow fast with low share — a bet on the future; Dogs are weak on both — usually divest. It gives a diversified firm a simple map of where money comes from and goes; its limits — that share equals strength and growth equals attractiveness — are why it is often paired with the GE nine-box, which swaps the axes for industry attractiveness and competitive strength.

oneLiner: 同时经营三条时间线：守住核心、押注成长、孵化未来，别让今天的成功饿死明天的机会。
oneLinerEn: Run three timelines at once — defend the core, build the growth, seed the future — so today's success does not starve tomorrow's.
detail: 增长的“三层面”框架由麦肯锡的巴盖伊等人于上世纪九十年代末至 2004 年间打磨成型，它把一个组织的增长拆成时间尺度迥异的三层：第一层是捍卫并优化的现金核心业务，靠效率与防守榨出当下利润；第二层是正在起量、需重点投资与培育的新增长业务，明天才收成；第三层则是高度不确定、却可能改写行业格局的长期期权与实验。真正的要害不在“做一份三年计划”，而在于给三层各配独立的指标、节奏与负责人——核心看现金流与份额，成长业务看新客户与单位经济，探索业务只看学习与里程碑——否则第一层会凭它强势的短期数字把所有资源吸干，等主业见顶时公司才发现后继无人、无牌可打。
detailEn: McKinsey's Three Horizons framework, refined by Baghai and colleagues from the late 1990s through 2004, splits a firm's growth into three layers that live on very different clocks. Horizon 1 is the cash core to optimise and defend, squeezing out today's profit through efficiency; Horizon 2 is the fast-rising new business that needs real investment and tending before it pays off; Horizon 3 is the highly uncertain long-term option or experiment that could reshape the whole game. The crux is not producing a three-year plan but giving each horizon its own metrics, cadence and owner — the core judged on cash and share, the growth business on new customers and unit economics, the ventures on learning and milestones — otherwise Horizon 1, with its overpowering short-term numbers, devours every resource, and by the time the core plateaus the firm finds it has no next card left to play.

oneLiner: 产量越大、单位成本越低——固定成本被摊薄，是低价与壁垒的常见来源。
oneLinerEn: The bigger the output, the lower the unit cost — fixed costs spread thin, a classic source of low price and entry barriers.
detail: 规模经济说的是：随着产量上升，单位成本因固定投入（厂房、研发、模具、平台）被摊得更薄、采购与议价也更划算而持续下降。这正是重资产工厂、软件与平台的一道天然护城河，也解释了为什么巨头能把价格压到对手跟不上、乃至导向“赢家通吃”。但它有边界：大到一定程度会转为“规模不经济”——层级臃肿、跨部门沟通成本飙升、官僚自我膨胀，反而把省下的钱吃回去。它与学习曲线、经验效应相关（越做越熟、越熟越省），但须小心区分“大”与“灵活”：大不等于强，臃肿的大一样脆弱。精益生产与模块化设计，正是为了兼得两者——既享有规模的低成本，又保留小团队的敏捷。
detailEn: Economies of scale are the fall in unit cost as output rises, because fixed inputs (plant, R&D, tooling, platform) spread thinner and purchasing gains bargaining power. This is a natural moat for heavy factories, software and platforms, and explains why a large player can push prices below what rivals can match, even tipping toward winner-takes-all. But there is a limit: past a certain size come diseconomies of scale — bloated layers, soaring cross-team communication cost and bureaucratic self-expansion eating back what was saved. It is kin to the learning and experience curve (more repetition, more mastery, less cost), yet big must be weighed against nimble: big is not strong, and a bloated giant is just as fragile. Lean production and modular design exist to have it both ways — the low cost of scale and the agility of a small team.

oneLiner: 用的人越多、产品对每个人都越值钱——电话、平台与社交网络的增长引擎。
oneLinerEn: The more people use it, the more valuable it becomes to each user — the growth engine of phones, platforms and social networks.
detail: 梅特卡夫定律说，一个网络的价值约与节点数的平方成正比——连接到更多人，就让它对每个人都更值钱。当新增用户让老用户更受益（通讯录里朋友越多越有用、市场买卖双方越多越活跃、操作系统的应用越丰富越难离开），就会形成正反馈：越大越好用、越好用越吸引人，常导向赢家通吃与极高的进入壁垒，这正是平台估值的核心逻辑。但网络效应并非只往好处走：要警惕负面效应（拥堵、垃圾信息、劣币驱逐良币让体验变差），更要面对冷启动难题——没跨过最小临界规模前它并不自发运转，常见解法是先在窄场景或单边做透、人为造出稀缺、或补贴另一端。它与规模经济、转换成本、锁定效应相伴，是一道护城河，却并非定价权的唯一来源。
detailEn: Metcalfe's law holds that a network's value grows roughly with the square of its nodes — being connected to more people makes it more valuable to each. When each new user leaves existing ones better off (more contacts make an address book useful, more buyers and sellers enliven a market, a richer app ecosystem makes an operating system harder to leave), a positive loop forms: bigger is better and better attracts bigger, often tipping to winner-takes-all and towering entry barriers, which is the core logic behind platform valuations. But network effects do not only run favourably: beware negative ones (congestion, spam, bad money driving out good that degrade the experience) and face the cold-start problem — below a minimum critical mass the loop will not spin on its own, so common fixes nail one narrow use or one side first, engineer scarcity, or subsidise the other side. It travels with economies of scale, switching costs and lock-in, a moat rather than the sole source of pricing power.

oneLiner: 增长不是单次猛推,而是让一环推动下一环,飞轮越转越沉、越转越快。
oneLinerEn: Growth is not one big push but each step driving the next — a flywheel that gains momentum turn after turn.
detail: 吉姆·柯林斯在《从优秀到卓越》里借飞轮作喻：卓越公司几乎从不依赖某个戏剧性的“奇迹时刻”或一剂灵丹，而是把一连串成果沿同一个方向持续累积，像推动一个巨大沉重的飞轮，起初每一下都费力、几乎看不见动静，可只要方向不变、一下下叠加，轮子一旦转起来便积攒起势不可挡的动量；反面则是“厄运之轮”——频繁更换方向、追新热点，每次刚攒起的劲又被清零空转。亚马逊把这枚飞轮具象成自我强化的闭环：更低的价格带来更多顾客，更多顾客吸引更多卖家，更繁荣的卖家平台带来更优的规模与选品体验，于是成本进一步摊薄、又能再降价。它的告诫很直白：与其不断换赛道做减法式折腾，不如找到那台属于自己的、能自我强化的飞轮，然后死磕不放。
detailEn: In Good to Great, Jim Collins uses the flywheel: great companies almost never rely on a single dramatic "miracle moment" or magic pill, but compound a sequence of results along one consistent direction, like pushing a huge heavy wheel — each shove laborious at first with little visible motion, yet kept going the same way the wheel builds unstoppable momentum; the shadow image is the doom loop, where a firm thrashes between fashions and resets its own accumulated effort to zero each time. Amazon made the wheel concrete as a self-reinforcing loop: lower prices bring more customers, more customers attract more sellers, a livelier marketplace improves scale and selection, costs spread thinner, and prices can fall again. Its warning is blunt: rather than forever switching lanes and thrashing, find the one self-reinforcing flywheel that is truly yours and stay doggedly on it.

oneLiner: 把抽象战略画成一张因果图:学习成长支撑流程,流程创造客户,客户换来财务。
oneLinerEn: Draw the abstract strategy as one cause-and-effect map: learning fuels processes, processes create customer value, customers deliver financial results.
detail: 卡普兰与诺顿在平衡计分卡之后，又提出战略地图来补上“逻辑”这一环：他们用财务、客户、内部流程、学习与成长四个层面，把“价值究竟是怎么被创造出来的”串成一条自下而上支撑、自上而下展开的因果链——员工的能力与士气支撑起关键流程的顺畅运转，流程做出差异化的客户价值主张，客户满意与留存最终兑现为财务成果。它要破解的正是那种人人嘴上认同战略、却说不清“我这一环到底怎么贡献”的执行僵局：部门经理第一次能在同一张图上看到自己的活动如何汇入最终结果。它与平衡计分卡配套使用——地图讲因果逻辑，记分卡给可量度的指标——一张负责“为什么”，一张负责“测什么”。
detailEn: After the balanced scorecard, Kaplan and Norton added the strategy map to supply the missing logic. Across four perspectives — financial, customer, internal process, and learning-and-growth — it strings how value is actually created into one causal chain, building up from below and cascading down from above: employees' skills and morale underpin the smooth running of key processes, those processes deliver a differentiated customer value proposition, and customer satisfaction and retention finally convert into financial results. It targets the very stalemate where everyone nods at the strategy yet cannot say how their own link contributes: a department head can for the first time trace, on a single page, how their activity feeds the outcome. It pairs with the scorecard — the map tells the causal logic, the card supplies the measurable indicators — one owning "why," the other owning "what to measure."

oneLiner: 互联网让无数小众销量的总和,能抵得上甚至超过少数爆款——别只盯着头部。
oneLinerEn: Online, the sum of countless niche sellers can rival or beat a few blockbusters — do not chase only the hits.
detail: 克里斯·安德森二〇〇四年在《连线》杂志提出并成书指出：当仓储、分发与搜索的成本趋近于零，货架不再是稀缺资源，那些单量很小、却种类海量的“冷门”商品累计起来，竟能形成与少数头部热门相抗衡的巨大市场（亚马逊的实体书、Netflix、Spotify 的曲库皆靠此累积长尾收入）。它依赖三股力量：普及生产工具、降低分发摩擦、以智能筛选与推荐把消费者导向各自感兴趣的那段长尾。但须清醒：长尾并非取代头部——需求曲线依旧偏斜、“赢家通吃”的爆款反而更突出，畅销与冷门是互补而非互斥；可行的策略是“头部引流、尾部获利”兼得。对内容平台，长尾也带来质量稀释、发现成本与“信息茧房”的新问题。
detailEn: Chris Anderson proposed it in Wired in 2004 and then in a book: when storage, distribution and search fall toward zero cost, shelf space stops being scarce, and the vast set of tiny-selling uncommons adds up to a market that can rival the few head hits — Amazon's physical titles, Netflix's catalogue and Spotify's library all bank on this accumulated tail. It rests on three forces: proliferate the production tools, cut distribution friction, and use smart filtering and recommendation to guide each consumer toward the part of the tail they care about. But stay clear-eyed: the tail does not replace the head — demand stays skewed and winner-take-all blockbusters loom larger, hits and uncommons being complements rather than substitutes; the viable play is to funnel traffic from the head and profit from the tail. For content platforms the tail also brings quality dilution, discovery cost and filter-bubble problems.

oneLiner: 与其在产品上争高下，不如在顾客心智里占据一个简单、独特的位置——定位是先占心，不是先占货。
oneLinerEn: Rather than out-feature the product, claim one simple, distinct spot in the customer's mind — positioning wins the mind before the shelf.
detail: 由艾·里斯与杰克·特劳特在二十世纪七十年代提出：信息过载、心智容量有限，竞争的真正战场不在货架而在消费者头脑里那块狭小的位置。品牌应聚焦一个词、一个差异点，抢先占据并年复一年反复强化（如“安全”之于沃尔沃、“隔夜必达”之于快递、“便宜”之于沃尔玛）；若某个空位已被强者盘踞，就不要正面硬撼，而是重新定位对手、给自己腾出空位（当年大众甲壳虫反其道以“小”为卖点、七喜自称“非可乐”皆此法）。它强调做减法——敢于放弃部分诉求、甚至收窄产品线，以换取心智中的清晰与“第一”。它把营销重心从“产品更好”转向“认知不同”，与 SWOT、波特五力的外向分析互补，共同回答“顾客凭什么选中你”。
detailEn: Proposed by Al Ries and Jack Trout in the 1970s: amid information overload and the mind's limited capacity, the real battlefield is not the shelf but the small slot in the customer's head. A brand should focus on one word, one point of difference, seize it early and reinforce it year after year (safety for Volvo, overnight delivery for a courier, low price for Walmart); when a position is already held by a strong rival, do not charge head-on but reposition the rival to open a gap for yourself, as Volkswagen's be-a-small-car stance and 7-Up's uncola positioning did. It stresses subtraction — daring to drop some claims, even narrowing the line, to buy clarity and being-first in the mind. It shifts marketing's centre of gravity from being better to being different in perception, and complements the outside-in analysis of SWOT and Porter's five forces in answering why a customer should choose you.

oneLiner: 对每项资源四问：能否创造价值、是否稀缺、对手难不难模仿、组织能否善加利用——四问皆过才是持续优势。
oneLinerEn: Ask four things of each resource: does it create value, is it rare, is it costly to imitate, is the firm organised to exploit it — only a clean sweep of all four yields sustained advantage.
detail: 由巴尼在伊迪丝·彭罗斯资源观的基础上发展而成，把企业看作一束异质且难以转移的资源与能力。评估一项资源依次过四道筛——它能否创造价值或抓住机遇、是否稀缺（仅少数对手拥有）、对手模仿成本高不高（壁垒源于独特历史路径、因果模糊、或社会复杂性如文化与人际网络）、以及组织是否已配好流程与激励把它真正用起来；四问层层递进，结果分别对应竞争劣势、竞争持平、暂时优势，直至四问全通过才是持续竞争优势。它把“向内看”的视角补强了偏重外部行业结构的定位学派：真正的护城河多长在异质、难复制的隐性资源与能力上，而非一时的营销巧思或单项技术。局限是框架偏静态，“稀缺”与“难模仿”须放进具体竞争情境里判断。
detailEn: Developed by Barney on the resource-based view rooted in Edith Penrose, it treats the firm as a bundle of heterogeneous, hard-to-move resources and capabilities. Test each resource through four ordered screens — Value (does it create value or seize opportunity), Rarity (do only a few rivals hold it), Imperfect imitability (is it costly for rivals to copy, the barrier arising from unique historical path, causal ambiguity, or social complexity such as culture and interpersonal networks), and Organisation (is the firm actually configured with the processes and incentives to exploit it); the four questions build up, and the answers map to competitive disadvantage, parity, temporary advantage, and — only when all four pass — sustained advantage. It strengthens the outside-in positioning school with an inside-out lens: the real moat usually grows on heterogeneous, hard-to-copy tacit resources, not on a passing marketing trick or a single technology. Its limits: the frame is fairly static, and rare and costly-to-imitate must be judged inside a specific competitive context.

oneLiner: 好生意周围该有一道挡住竞争的壕沟——品牌、转换成本、网络效应或成本优势，让超额利润守得住。
oneLinerEn: A good business sits behind a moat that deters rivals — brand, switching cost, network effect or cost advantage — so excess returns can endure.
detail: 这个说法因巴菲特而广为人知，指的是一家企业可持续的结构性竞争优势，能把竞争者长期挡在高回报之外。常见的护城河有几种：无形资产（品牌、专利、监管牌照）、客户转换成本（换掉你太麻烦、太贵）、网络效应、成本优势，以及在细分市场里“一家就够”的高效规模。检验它的终极标准是定价权——能不能提价而不流失客户；有，说明护城河真实存在，没有，多半只是暂时的运营之利。但护城河并非一劳永逸：技术更迭、政策变化、消费习惯迁移都可能一点点把它填平——曾经的行业霸主被后来者越过的事并不罕见。所以战略与投资都要反复分辨同一件事——这条优势究竟在变宽还是变窄，此刻挖深它的最有效动作又是什么。
detailEn: The phrase was popularised by Buffett and names a firm's durable structural advantage that keeps rivals locked out of its high returns over years. Common moats are intangible assets (brand, patents, regulatory licences), customer switching costs (it is too costly or painful to leave), network effects, cost advantage, and the efficient scale where one player suffices for a niche. The final test is pricing power — can you raise prices without losing customers; if yes the moat is real, if no what you have is likely a temporary operational edge. Yet no moat is permanent: technology shifts, policy changes and migrating taste can each fill it in little by little, and once-dominant firms being overtaken is far from rare. So strategy and investing alike must keep answering one question — is this advantage widening or narrowing, and what is the most effective move to deepen it right now.

oneLiner: 任何增长曲线终会见顶；要在第一曲线尚未衰败时，就提前投入那条全新的第二曲线。
oneLinerEn: Every growth curve eventually tops out; start the new second curve before the first one declines.
detail: 由管理哲学家查尔斯·汉迪提出、后经德格斯在《长寿公司》中用于组织变革：S 形曲线描述事物从投入、起飞、加速、成熟到衰退的轨迹，而最危险的时刻恰是巅峰——既得利益、成功惯性“这套还能再赚几年”的心态会让人拒绝改变，等曲线见顶再转往往为时已晚。因此第二曲线必须在第一曲线仍处上升、资源尚充足、现金流还能反哺时就播下种子，尽管它初期看起来更小、更不划算，会分流注意力、与现有业务争夺资源，并常触发克里斯坦森所谓“创新者的窘境”。它考验领导者的关键正在于：能否在成功如日中天、无人报警时主动自我颠覆、克制“收割第一曲线”的诱惑。柯达、诺基亚的教训皆在于见顶才转身。
detailEn: Raised by the management philosopher Charles Handy and applied to organisations by de Geus in The Living Company: the S-curve traces a rise from investment, take-off, acceleration, maturity to decline, and the most dangerous moment is the peak itself, when vested interest, the inertia of success and the thought “this will keep paying for a few more years” make people refuse to change — turning only once the curve has crested is usually too late. The second curve must therefore be seeded while the first is still climbing, resources are plentiful and cash flow can still fund it, even though it looks smaller and less worthwhile early on, splits attention, competes with the core for resources, and often triggers what Christensen called the innovator's dilemma. The defining test of leadership is whether, at the height of success with no alarm ringing, one dares to self-disrupt and resist the temptation to simply harvest the first curve — Kodak and Nokia failed by turning only at the top.
